_comment: Curated per-paper analysis fields for the 'Literature Analysis' sheet. Every entry is grounded in the verified metadata plus the paper abstract retrieved during verification; where the abstract does not state a field, the value is the explicit string 'Not stated in retrieved abstract' rather than a guess. Fields that this project codes itself (weather_regime_eval, statistical_test, code_released, dataset_public, cost_reported) are booleans derived from abstract text and are the basis for the evidence counts in docs/research_gaps.md.

coded_fields_legend.weather_regime_eval: Paper reports accuracy broken down by named weather condition(s).
coded_fields_legend.statistical_test: Paper applies a formal significance test for model comparison.
coded_fields_legend.code_released: Paper states public code is available.
coded_fields_legend.dataset_public: Paper states the dataset is publicly available.
coded_fields_legend.cost_reported: Paper reports training/inference cost, runtime or parameter count.

G1.forecast_horizon: Short-term (day-ahead to sub-day); horizon grid not enumerated in abstract
G1.dataset: Literature corpus plus authors' own ML simulation on PV data
G1.input_variables: Not enumerated in retrieved abstract; reviewed models use PV history and meteorological inputs
G1.weather_variables: Meteorological inputs discussed in reviewed studies (irradiance, temperature, cloud cover among them)
G1.specific_model: Multiple ML methods simulated by the authors for comparison; exact list not in abstract
G1.baselines: Persistence and previously published ML methods (as reviewed)
G1.weather_conditions_considered: Reviewed literature covers multiple conditions; no controlled regime evaluation in the review itself
G1.main_contribution: Comprehensive comparative review of ML-based short-term PV power forecasting, plus an independent simulation comparing ML methods to add evidence beyond the surveyed papers.
G1.main_limitation: Review-level aggregation; models are compared across heterogeneous studies rather than on a common dataset and split, so cross-study numbers are not directly comparable.
G1.research_gap: Demonstrates the absence of a common-dataset benchmark; authors resort to their own simulation because the literature does not permit controlled comparison.
G1.reproducibility: Partial - review methodology described; reviewed studies' code not assessed

G2.forecast_horizon: Surveyed across studies; not fixed by the review
G2.dataset: 26 selected studies screened from 155 Web of Science records
G2.dataset_location: Web of Science (literature corpus, not a PV dataset)
G2.input_variables: Ambient temperature, pressure and humidity reported as the most common input features across surveyed studies
G2.weather_variables: Ambient temperature, pressure, humidity (most common); Wavelet Transform most common decomposition; Pearson correlation most common feature selection
G2.specific_model: LSTM (32.69% of papers), CNN (28.85%); further architectures not enumerated in abstract
G2.baselines: Not applicable (review); baselines of surveyed studies are not aggregated in the abstract
G2.metrics: Surveyed metrics catalogued but not enumerated in the retrieved abstract
G2.weather_conditions_considered: Identified as a persistent challenge; no regime-stratified synthesis reported in the abstract
G2.uncertainty: Identified as a persistent challenge; not itself quantified
G2.main_contribution: Systematic literature review (155 -> 26 papers) quantifying which DL architectures, preprocessing techniques, input features, metrics and challenges dominate solar/PV forecasting.
G2.main_limitation: Corpus restricted to Web of Science; reported architecture frequencies describe the literature's choices, not their measured superiority.
G2.research_gap: Quantifies the field's concentration on LSTM/CNN and identifies preprocessing, metrics and persistent challenges as under-examined dimensions.
G2.reproducibility: Good - explicit inclusion/exclusion counts, database and frequencies reported

G3.forecast_horizon: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.dataset: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.dataset_location: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.dataset_size: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.sampling_frequency: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.input_variables: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.weather_variables: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.specific_model: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.baselines: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.metrics: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.weather_conditions_considered: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.explainability: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.uncertainty: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.multi_site_validation: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.external_validation: Not stated - abstract not publicly retrievable
G3.main_contribution: Comprehensive review of deep learning models for solar irradiance forecasting (title and venue verified; 394 citations per Semantic Scholar).
G3.main_limitation: PROVENANCE LIMITATION: the abstract is not available from Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, the publisher landing page or any RePEc mirror (paywalled), so no claim beyond verified bibliographic metadata is asserted here. Full-text consultation is required before citing this work for any specific methodological or numerical detail.
G3.research_gap: Not assessable without full text; flagged as unverified rather than characterised.

G4.dataset: Two-year 15-min resolution measurements from 16 PV plants
G4.dataset_size: 16 PV plants x 2 years at 15-min resolution (exact record count not stated in abstract)
G4.input_variables: Numerical weather prediction variables; augmented with Sun position angles and statistically processed irradiance values
G4.weather_variables: NWP-derived variables plus solar position angles and processed irradiance
G4.specific_model: 24 models compared; best two are kernel ridge regression and multilayer perceptron; linear regression used as the baseline scenario
G4.baselines: Persistence; linear regression; 24 models in total
G4.metrics: RMSE, forecast skill score relative to persistence
G4.best_reported_metric: Up to 44.6% forecast skill score over persistence (kernel ridge regression and MLP); best forecasts 13.9% lower RMSE than the linear-regression baseline
G4.weather_conditions_considered: Two-year continuous evaluation implicitly spans seasons; no explicit regime stratification reported in the abstract
G4.explainability: No (predictor-selection effects reported, which is a form of sensitivity analysis rather than post-hoc explanation)
G4.multi_site_validation: Yes - 16 plants, though pooled rather than as transfer tests
G4.external_validation: Yes - two-year span with chronological hold-out implied by the forecast setup
G4.main_contribution: Largest controlled classical-ML comparison in this corpus: 24 models, 16 plants, two years, with explicit quantification of predictor-selection and hyperparameter-tuning effects.
G4.main_limitation: Classical ML only - no deep or transformer architectures included, so the study cannot settle whether modern architectures beat well-tuned classical models.
G4.research_gap: Sets the classical-ML bar (persistence skill) that deep-learning PV papers frequently do not report, making cross-paper comparison impossible.
G4.reproducibility: Good - dataset scale, model count, baselines and metric definitions all stated; code availability not stated in abstract

A1.dataset: Measurements from one PV power plant
A1.input_variables: Meteorological and PV factors ranked by Random Forest importance
A1.weather_variables: Meteorological factors affecting PV generation (specific list not in abstract)
A1.model_family: Hybrid: feature selection + decomposition + neural network
A1.specific_model: RF-CEEMD-DIFPSO-BPNN (Random Forest importance, CEEMD decomposition, PSO-optimised backpropagation NN)
A1.baselines: Contemporary ML/DL models (specific list not in abstract)
A1.metrics: Forecast accuracy metrics (specific list not enumerated in abstract)
A1.best_reported_metric: Not stated numerically in retrieved abstract
A1.weather_conditions_considered: Weather-type grouping used for similar-day screening (IGIVA); not a full regime evaluation
A1.explainability: Partial - Random Forest importance ranking reported
A1.main_contribution: End-to-end hybrid pipeline coupling RF-based factor ranking, weather-type similar-day screening, CEEMD decomposition and PSO-tuned BPNN.
A1.main_limitation: Single-plant case study with a five-stage pipeline, so it is difficult to attribute gains to any single component; no ablation isolating contributions.
A1.research_gap: Composite pipelines without component-level ablation make the contribution of each stage unattributable.
A1.reproducibility: Low - many interacting stages, no code or parameter detail in abstract

A2.dataset: 1 MW PV plant measurements plus numerically predicted weather variables
A2.dataset_size: One 1-MW plant, 1 year of hourly forecasts
A2.input_variables: Numerically predicted weather variables including cloudiness
A2.weather_variables: Cloudiness and other numerically predicted weather variables
A2.specific_model: Support Vector Regression / support vector machine methodology
A2.baselines: Variant of the same model without cloudiness input (an internal ablation)
A2.metrics: RMSE, MAE, correlation between forecast and measured power
A2.best_reported_metric: RMSE 0.0948 MWh, MAE 0.058 MWh; correlation 0.80-0.88 by season; removing cloudiness raises RMSE by more than 32% and MAE by more than 42%
A2.weather_conditions_considered: Seasonal stratification (correlation reported by season); cloudiness as an explicit predictor
A2.main_contribution: Clean quantification of a single physically meaningful predictor's value: numerically forecast cloudiness is decisive for SVR PV forecasting.
A2.main_limitation: Single 1-MW plant, hourly resolution only; no comparison against deep models, so conclusions are SVR-specific.
A2.research_gap: Shows weather-predictor quality can dominate model choice, yet later deep-learning papers rarely ablate individual weather inputs.
A2.reproducibility: Moderate - plant, resolution, duration and metrics all stated

A3.dataset: Actual database collected from weather sensors for a distributed PV system
A3.input_variables: Weather measurements; a voted feature-weighting vector is constructed from attribute-selection ensembles
A3.weather_variables: Weather sensor measurements (specific list not in abstract)
A3.model_family: Classical machine learning + explainability-driven feature engineering
A3.specific_model: Enhanced Random Forest with ensemble attribute selection (LIME, Extreme Boosting, Elastic Net)
A3.metrics: Forecast accuracy metrics (specific list not in abstract)
A3.best_reported_metric: Not stated numerically in retrieved abstract
A3.weather_conditions_considered: Motivated by sudden variations from stochastic weather; no named regime stratification reported
A3.explainability: Yes - LIME used inside the feature-weighting procedure (explanations used to build the model, not only to interpret it)
A3.multi_site_validation: No - a typical distributed PV system
A3.main_contribution: Uses interpretability methods as a functional component of model construction (voted feature weighting) rather than as post-hoc commentary.
A3.main_limitation: Explainability is instrumentalised for feature selection, so it does not provide a faithful account of the final fitted model's behaviour.
A3.research_gap: Illustrates that XAI is used as a build tool rather than as a validation instrument; no XAI-based verification that explanations match model behaviour.
A3.reproducibility: Moderate - methods named, dataset not shared per abstract

A4.input_variables: Meteorological and operational parameters: temperature, humidity, wind profile, cloudiness distribution, solar situation
A4.weather_variables: Temperature, humidity, wind profile, cloudiness, solar position
A4.specific_model: Gradient Boosting + XGBoost base learners with Ridge Regression meta-learner
A4.baselines: Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, multilayer perceptron, LSTM; evaluated with k-fold cross-validation
A4.weather_conditions_considered: Cloudiness used as an input; no regime-stratified results reported in abstract
A4.uncertainty: Partial - dispersion reported across k-fold repeats (MAE +/- 0.002), which is variability not calibrated prediction intervals
A4.external_validation: No - k-fold cross-validation, which is not a temporal hold-out
A4.main_contribution: Stacked GB-XGBoost ensemble with ridge meta-learner, benchmarked against four boosting variants, an MLP and an LSTM with nonparametric tests.
A4.main_limitation: Uses k-fold cross-validation on a time series, which leaks temporal information and inflates apparent accuracy relative to a chronological hold-out; this is a methodological weakness shared by much of the boosting literature.
A4.research_gap: Direct evidence that random-fold validation is common in applied PV ML, making reported gains incomparable with chronological-split studies such as G4.
A4.reproducibility: Moderate - pipeline and comparison set described; normalisation and feature selection named

B1.input_variables: PV time-series history (temporal and spatial feature extraction)
B1.specific_model: LSTM-Convolutional Network (temporal features by LSTM first, then spatial features by CNN)
B1.baselines: Standalone LSTM, standalone CNN, and the Convolutional-LSTM ordering (CNN first, then LSTM)
B1.best_reported_metric: Hybrid outperforms both single models and the reversed Conv-LSTM ordering (numbers not in abstract)
B1.main_contribution: Establishes and empirically justifies the ordering of recurrent-then-convolutional feature extraction against the reversed ordering, a control often omitted elsewhere.
B1.main_limitation: Single dataset with no persistence reference reported, so the absolute gain over a trivial baseline cannot be judged.
B1.research_gap: No strong-baseline reference (persistence) reported, so headline hybrid gains are unanchored.
B1.reproducibility: Low to moderate - architecture described, code and data not released per abstract

B2.forecast_horizon: Day-ahead hourly (sunshine hours of a day predicted jointly)
B2.dataset_size: Three sites; exact record counts not stated in abstract
B2.input_variables: Multivariate series decomposed by NA-MEMD into intrinsic mode functions
B2.weather_variables: Multivariate weather series (specific list not in abstract)
B2.specific_model: NA-MEMD decomposition with one LSTM per set of multivariate IMFs, jointly predicting the target IMF for a full day
B2.metrics: RMSE, MAE (reported as percentage reductions); also decomposition runtime
B2.best_reported_metric: Average RMSE 65.08 W/m2 across three locations; %RMSE (%MAE) reduction of 47.65 (50.99) vs standalone LSTM and 11.11 (15.76) vs MEMD-LSTM
B2.weather_conditions_considered: Three locations imply differing climates; no explicit regime stratification reported
B2.external_validation: Partial - three sites, but all used within the same train/test protocol rather than as transfer tests
B2.main_contribution: Decomposition-based day-ahead multi-step forecasting with a per-IMF LSTM design, plus a decomposition-cost comparison (NA-MEMD 195 s vs MEMD 251 s).
B2.main_limitation: Target reported in W/m2 (irradiance units) rather than PV power, so comparability with power-forecasting studies is limited; decomposition adds a substantial preprocessing stage.
B2.research_gap: One of the few studies reporting preprocessing cost alongside accuracy, yet the accuracy gain is confounded with an added decomposition stage that itself requires tuning.
B2.reproducibility: Moderate - decomposition and architecture described with runtimes

B3.forecast_target: Global horizontal irradiance (GHI) and derived PV power
B3.dataset: Weather and irradiance measurements with k-means weather typing
B3.dataset_location: Not stated in retrieved abstract (cross-regional study performed)
B3.input_variables: Multivariate sequence plus clearness index used to classify weather type
B3.weather_variables: GHI, clearness index, and other multivariate weather variables
B3.baselines: RNN; ANN and SVR cited from literature for cloudy-day behaviour
B3.metrics: R2 (plus other indices not enumerated in abstract)
B3.best_reported_metric: R2 reported for hourly and daily forecasts (values truncated in retrieved abstract)
B3.weather_conditions_considered: Yes - k-means weather classification into clear, cloudy and mixed/partially cloudy, motivated by cloudy-day error
B3.multi_site_validation: Yes - explicit cross-regional study to test generalisability
B3.external_validation: Yes - cross-regional transfer is the stated purpose
B3.main_contribution: Introduces clearness index as an LSTM input and combines k-means weather typing with a cross-regional generalisation test.
B3.main_limitation: Forecasts irradiance rather than PV power directly, and the weather classes are derived from an input feature (clearness index) rather than an independent physical classification.
B3.research_gap: Weather-regime evaluation is present but the regime labels are derived from the same signal being forecast, which can confound regime-wise error analysis.
B3.reproducibility: Moderate - method described; code not released per abstract

B4.dataset: One-year database of PV output history and sky images
B4.dataset_size: 1 year of data at minutely resolution (exact count not stated)
B4.input_variables: Hybrid input: PV output history plus sky images; lag-term configuration studied explicitly
B4.weather_variables: Sky images; cloud movement is the driver of forecast uncertainty
B4.specific_model: SUNSET - a specialised CNN with hybrid input and strong regularisation
B4.baselines: Smart persistence forecast (explicit reference); input and output configuration variants
B4.metrics: Forecast skill relative to smart persistence, stratified by cloudy vs all-weather
B4.best_reported_metric: 16.3% forecast skill in cloudy conditions and 15.7% in all weather relative to smart persistence
B4.weather_conditions_considered: Yes - cloudy versus all-weather skill reported
B4.main_contribution: Systematic study of input and output configuration (history length, downsampling, PV-output versus clear-sky-index targets) with results reported as skill over smart persistence, plus public code.
B4.main_limitation: Single site and one year; requires sky images, which many operational sites lack.
B4.research_gap: Rare example of a rigorous, openly reproducible study anchored to a smart-persistence reference - precisely the practice this corpus otherwise lacks.
B4.reproducibility: High - code publicly released on GitHub (YuchiSun/SUNSET) and configuration recommendations stated

C1.input_variables: Statistical wavelet-transform features of the time series plus temperature, wind speed, pressure, cloudy index, humidity, altimeter index
C1.weather_variables: Temperature, wind speed, pressure, cloudy index, humidity, altimeter index
C1.specific_model: WT-LSTM: wavelet transform decomposition plus statistical feature extraction, then dropout-regularised LSTM
C1.baselines: Contemporary machine learning and deep learning models
C1.best_reported_metric: Not stated numerically in retrieved abstract
C1.weather_conditions_considered: Cloudy index used as an input; no regime-stratified evaluation reported
C1.main_contribution: Couples wavelet-domain feature extraction with an LSTM and evaluates at two horizons (hourly and daily).
C1.main_limitation: Reports MAPE on a target that is zero at night, which makes the percentage metric unstable; no night-time masking described in the abstract.
C1.research_gap: Exemplifies inconsistent metric practice: MAPE is reported without justification despite a target containing exact zeros.

C2.dataset: Multi-source data: local measurements, NWP and satellite images, from 50 PV power stations
C2.dataset_location: 50 real-world PV power stations (region not stated in abstract)
C2.input_variables: Time-series records plus satellite images; local measurements and NWP
C2.weather_variables: Satellite imagery, NWP fields, local sensor measurements
C2.specific_model: U-Net combined with an encoder-decoder architecture, cooperatively processing time-series and image data
C2.baselines: Several baseline models (not enumerated in abstract)
C2.best_reported_metric: Reported as higher accuracy than baselines across 50 stations (numbers not in abstract)
C2.main_contribution: Demonstrates that fusing satellite imagery with local time series via U-Net plus encoder-decoder improves intra-hour forecasting, validated at unusual scale (50 stations).
C2.main_limitation: Requires satellite imagery, which imposes latency and licensing constraints for real-time operation; accuracy figures are not recoverable from the abstract.
C2.research_gap: Multi-source models are evaluated at scale but their dependence on exogenous imagery makes latency and cost trade-offs unexamined.
C2.reproducibility: Moderate - architecture and station count given; data access not described

C3.dataset: Actual data from a 1 MW PV power station
C3.dataset_size: One 1-MW station (record count not stated in abstract)
C3.input_variables: Multidimensional time-series features with learned feature extraction and attention weighting
C3.weather_variables: Multidimensional weather time series (specific list not in abstract)
C3.best_reported_metric: Ablation: removing the CNN component increased MAE by 58.2% and RMSE by 53.9%; removing attention increased maximum error by 83.8%
C3.weather_conditions_considered: Weather variability is the stated motivation; no regime-stratified results reported in the abstract
C3.main_contribution: Component-level ablation quantifying the contribution of the CNN stage and the attention mechanism separately - one of the few papers in this corpus that isolates architectural components.
C3.main_limitation: Single station; relative percentage changes are reported without absolute error levels, making practical significance unclear.
C3.research_gap: Shows ablation is possible and informative, yet the paper still reports only relative degradation rather than absolute calibrated errors, and does not test robustness across regimes or sites.

C4.dataset: Target station NWP data plus highly correlated features from nearby PV stations
C4.dataset_size: Target station plus a set of selected neighbouring stations (count not stated in abstract)
C4.input_variables: NWP data of the target station plus correlated features from nearby stations, selected via a distance-weighted similarity index and fused at a Bayesian-optimised ratio
C4.weather_variables: NWP fields and neighbouring-station irradiance/power features
C4.specific_model: Conv-LSTM-ATT with Bayesian-optimised multi-station data fusion
C4.best_reported_metric: Data fusion reduces test RMSE by 20.04% (sunny), 28.24% (cloudy) and 30.94% (rainy)
C4.weather_conditions_considered: Yes - sunny, cloudy and rainy conditions reported separately
C4.explainability: Partial - station similarity index and fusion ratio provide an interpretable selection mechanism
C4.external_validation: Partial - neighbouring stations supply inputs; the model is not transferred to unseen sites
C4.main_contribution: Quantifies how much neighbouring-station data fusion helps, and reports the benefit separately for sunny, cloudy and rainy conditions.
C4.main_limitation: Fusion assumes neighbouring stations are available and correlated at inference time; no test of generalisation to sites absent from the training pool.
C4.research_gap: Demonstrates the value of spatial context while leaving open whether a model trained on a station pool generalises to a new site - the transfer question remains unaddressed.
C4.reproducibility: Moderate - selection index and optimisation procedure described

C5.forecast_horizon: Short-term (days), compared against medium and long-term (months)
C5.dataset: Daily PV power generation from Xuhui District, Shanghai, plus DKASC Alice Springs data
C5.dataset_location: Shanghai, China and Alice Springs, Australia
C5.sampling_frequency: Daily (with monthly aggregation for medium/long-term comparison)
C5.input_variables: Daily generation smoothed by LOWESS, plus natural factors selected by Random Forest
C5.weather_variables: Natural factors affecting daily generation (specific list not in abstract)
C5.model_family: Hybrid: smoothing + feature selection + recurrent deep learning
C5.specific_model: Improved GRU with RepeatVector and TimeDistributed layers, on LOWESS-smoothed, RF-selected inputs
C5.baselines: Three prediction models (not enumerated in abstract); original GRU as the base model
C5.metrics: Forecast error metrics (not enumerated in abstract)
C5.best_reported_metric: Not stated numerically in retrieved abstract
C5.explainability: Partial - Random Forest used for feature selection
C5.external_validation: Yes - second dataset used to test short vs medium/long-term suitability
C5.main_contribution: Compares five smoothing techniques head-to-head, adds RF feature selection, and augments GRU with RepeatVector/TimeDistributed layers; tests the method on a second, climatically distinct dataset.
C5.main_limitation: Operates at daily resolution, which sidesteps the intra-day ramping problem that dominates operational PV forecasting relevance.
C5.research_gap: Cross-site validation is used to justify generality, but at a temporal resolution too coarse to answer questions about intra-day robustness.
C5.reproducibility: Moderate - all processing stages enumerated; no code released per abstract

C6.dataset: Field validation at a 150 kW PV power plant
C6.dataset_size: One 150-kW plant (record count not stated in abstract)
C6.input_variables: Time-series features with SE-based (squeeze-and-excitation) dynamic attention weighting
C6.weather_variables: Meteorological inputs (specific list not in abstract)
C6.baselines: Standard LSTM; CNN-LSTM (suboptimal baseline); further baselines not enumerated
C6.metrics: RMSE, Diebold-Mariano test, Dynamic Time Warping, residual distribution analysis
C6.best_reported_metric: RMSE convergence of 2.157 kW; 41.92% reduction vs standard LSTM; 16.46% improvement over the CNN-LSTM baseline
C6.explainability: No - attention weights are used for weighting, not interpreted
C6.main_contribution: One of very few papers in this corpus that applies a Diebold-Mariano test and analyses residual distributions to support a superiority claim, and quantifies the attention module's marginal contribution.
C6.main_limitation: Single small (150 kW) plant; the DM test details (loss function, horizon, sample size) are not recoverable from the abstract.
C6.research_gap: Demonstrates that significance testing is achievable in applied PV forecasting, yet remains isolated - this corpus contains no other paper that formally tests model differences.
C6.reproducibility: Moderate - tests and metrics named; code not released per abstract

D1.dataset: Data from two PV power plants
D1.dataset_size: Two PV plants (record counts not stated in abstract)
D1.input_variables: Historical solar power generation, weather observation, weather forecast and solar geometry data
D1.weather_variables: Weather observations, weather forecasts, solar geometry (solar position angles)
D1.specific_model: PVTransNet - three transformer variants, the third (PVTransNet-EDR) combining LSTM with the transformer to supplement weather-station forecasts
D1.baselines: Individual LSTM; other transformer variants; traditional operational benchmarks implied
D1.metrics: MAE (primary), plus other metrics not enumerated in abstract
D1.best_reported_metric: PVTransNet-EDR performed 48.3% better in MAE than simple LSTM
D1.explainability: No - solar geometry is an input, not an explanation
D1.external_validation: Partial - two plants, but not framed as cross-site transfer
D1.main_contribution: Shows that combining an LSTM encoder with a transformer, and adding solar geometry alongside weather data, yields large day-ahead gains over plain LSTM on two plants.
D1.main_limitation: The 48.3% MAE improvement is against plain LSTM rather than a tuned classical baseline, so it does not establish superiority over well-tuned gradient boosting.
D1.research_gap: Advanced architectures are typically compared against weak neural baselines, not against tuned classical ML with persistence-relative skill, leaving their true margin unestablished.
D1.reproducibility: Moderate - inputs and variants described; code not released per abstract

D2.dataset: OpenMeteo meteorological data combined with an irradiance model
D2.dataset_location: OpenMeteo (open meteorological data provider); site not stated in abstract
D2.input_variables: Irradiance from a meteorological provider, local weather data, modelled irradiance and PV plant configuration data
D2.weather_variables: Provider meteorological forecasts and modelled irradiance
D2.specific_model: Transformer Neural Network trained on OpenMeteo data
D2.baselines: Other machine learning techniques and other meteorological forecast providers, systematically compared
D2.weather_conditions_considered: Meteorological provider comparison acts as a proxy for condition sensitivity; no named regime stratification reported
D2.main_contribution: Systematically quantifies the effect of the meteorological forecast provider on PV forecasting accuracy, decoupling accuracy from model architecture.
D2.main_limitation: Reports MAPE on a target that is zero outside daylight hours; the irradiance model is coupled to a single provider, so results depend on that provider's skill.
D2.research_gap: Isolates input-source quality as a confounder of model comparison - an important control that most architecture-focused papers omit, yet rarely combined with persistence-anchored skill.
D2.reproducibility: Good - open data source (OpenMeteo) named, provider comparison explicit

D3.dataset: Multi-site PV power data at multiple temporal scales via average downsampling
D3.sampling_frequency: Multi-scale (minute-level and hourly scales constructed by downsampling)
D3.input_variables: Historical PV power from multiple sites; graphs from geographic topology and self-learned adjacency matrices
D3.weather_variables: Historical PV power sequences (weather variables not the primary input)
D3.model_family: Graph neural network / spatial-temporal deep learning
D3.specific_model: MSF-GCN - Multi-Scale Fused Graph Convolutional Network with Multi-Graph Convolution (MGCN), Decomposed-Bidirectional-Fusion (DBF) MLP block and multiple unshared-weight predictors
D3.baselines: Existing multi-site and spatiotemporal methods (not enumerated in abstract)
D3.metrics: Accuracy metrics plus run-time efficiency; ablation per block
D3.best_reported_metric: Consistent accuracy improvement over existing methods with favourable run-time efficiency (numbers not in abstract)
D3.weather_conditions_considered: Not stated in retrieved abstract; inter-site correlation variation across time scales is the explicit focus
D3.explainability: Partial - learned adjacency matrices and per-block ablations provide architectural interpretability
D3.multi_site_validation: Yes - multi-site modelling is the core contribution
D3.external_validation: No - models sites jointly rather than testing transfer to unseen sites
D3.main_contribution: Formalises the observation that inter-site correlation strength is time-scale dependent (geographic at hourly scales, decorrelated at minute scales) and builds a multi-scale graph architecture around it, with per-block ablation.
D3.main_limitation: Requires a dense multi-site panel with aligned measurements, which many operators lack; the architecture is complex, raising the computational bar without a cost/accuracy frontier analysis.
D3.research_gap: Multi-site work optimises joint modelling but does not quantify the accuracy-versus-complexity trade-off, nor test whether a model trained on a site pool transfers to an unseen site.
D3.reproducibility: Moderate - architecture and ablations detailed; data access not described

D4.forecast_target: Residential PV power production (low-volume, univariate time series)
D4.dataset: Low-volume residential PV production time series
D4.dataset_size: Not stated in retrieved abstract; characterised as low-volume
D4.weather_variables: None - univariate setting (an explicit and unusual design choice)
D4.specific_model: XGBoost, random forest, SVR, multilayer perceptron, tuned LSTM, and a proposed ConvLSTM1D
D4.baselines: The other five models in the benchmark; results considered alongside technical and economic impacts
D4.best_reported_metric: Random forest and ConvLSTM1D yielded the most accurate performance (lowest RMSE, MAPE, MAE) across scenarios
D4.main_contribution: Univariate benchmark of six models on low-volume residential PV, and notably finds random forest competitive with the best deep model - an important counterweight to deep-learning dominance.
D4.main_limitation: Univariate inputs discard weather information, so accuracy is capped; reported MAPE on a zero-containing target is not justified.
D4.research_gap: Provides direct evidence that a classical ensemble can match a deep architecture, reinforcing that deep models are not automatically superior - a claim most PV forecasting papers do not test.
D4.reproducibility: Moderate - model list and metrics explicit; data not shared per abstract

D5.dataset: Measurements from two PV arrays: poly-crystalline (Array 1) and mono-crystalline (Array 2)
D5.dataset_location: Tropical climate (region not named in abstract)
D5.dataset_size: Two arrays (record counts not stated in abstract)
D5.input_variables: Time-indexed series used with a recursive forecasting strategy
D5.weather_variables: Meteorological inputs (specific list not in abstract)
D5.specific_model: Sequential GRU-LSTM hybrid with GRU as the primary connector passing short-term dependencies to an LSTM layer, with recursive forecasting
D5.baselines: Standalone ML and DL models, including standalone GRU and LSTM
D5.best_reported_metric: Array 1: RMSE 28.55 W, MAE 19.43 W, R2 0.9961
D5.weather_conditions_considered: Tropical climatic variability is the stated context; no named regime stratification reported
D5.multi_site_validation: Partial - two co-located arrays of different technology, which tests technology transfer rather than geographic transfer
D5.main_contribution: Tests a GRU-LSTM sequential hybrid under recursive forecasting and compares two PV technologies, which probes whether architecture conclusions are technology-dependent.
D5.main_limitation: Recursive multi-step prediction accumulates error; a very high R2 (0.9961) on a single array is not evidence of robustness under regime change.
D5.research_gap: Near-perfect aggregate R2 coexists with no regime, seasonal or cross-site analysis - direct evidence that aggregate metrics can mask operational failure modes.
D5.reproducibility: Moderate - architecture and metrics explicit; data not shared per abstract

E1.input_variables: Selected via a two-stage hybrid sensitivity analysis; includes PV domain knowledge as constraints
E1.weather_variables: PV domain knowledge and meteorological inputs (specific list not in abstract)
E1.specific_model: PC-LSTM - physics-constrained LSTM enforcing PV physical consistency
E1.baselines: Standard LSTM; data-only machine learning models
E1.metrics: Forecast accuracy and robustness (not enumerated in abstract)
E1.best_reported_metric: PC-LSTM stronger than standard LSTM, more robust and better suited to sparse-data settings (numbers not in abstract)
E1.weather_conditions_considered: Robustness emphasised; no named regime stratification reported
E1.explainability: Partial - physical constraints make behaviour interpretable by construction
E1.main_contribution: Introduces a physics-constrained LSTM that prevents physically unreasonable forecasts and claims improved robustness and data efficiency, targeting a known failure mode of pure data-driven models.
E1.main_limitation: Constraint design and penalty weighting are not described in the abstract, so the mechanism behind the gains cannot be assessed; robustness claims are not tied to a formal regime protocol.
E1.research_gap: Physics-informed models claim robustness benefits but do not quantify them against a transparent weather-regime protocol, leaving the central claim untested.
E1.reproducibility: Low to moderate - constraint mechanism not detailed in abstract; code not released per abstract

E2.dataset: One-year time series of solar power generation plus panel physical features and weather information
E2.dataset_size: One year of time series; multiple plants in validation
E2.input_variables: Solar generation time series, solar panel physical features and weather information
E2.weather_variables: Weather information (specific list not in abstract)
E2.specific_model: Deep learning ensemble based on Bi-LSTM, incorporating domain knowledge and panel physical characteristics
E2.baselines: Multiple standard deep learning models and traditional models
E2.best_reported_metric: Reported as better than traditional models on both short and long horizons (numbers not in abstract)
E2.explainability: Partial - physical panel features and domain knowledge are explicit inputs
E2.multi_site_validation: Yes - validated on different solar plants in Durgapur, India
E2.main_contribution: Integrates panel physical characteristics alongside weather and generation history, and claims the model forecasts well regardless of geographical position.
E2.main_limitation: The generalisation claim is supported by validation at a second site within one city and climate, which is a weak test of geographic generalisation; long-horizon claims are not quantified in the abstract.
E2.research_gap: 'Generalises regardless of location' is asserted from same-climate validation - the corpus contains no true cross-climate transfer experiment to test such claims.
E2.reproducibility: Low to moderate - inputs described qualitatively; code not released per abstract

E3.dataset: DKASC Alice Springs dataset, four different data sequences
E3.dataset_size: Four data sequences from the DKASC dataset (record counts not stated in abstract)
E3.input_variables: PV generation and associated inputs across four data sequences
E3.weather_variables: Meteorological inputs from the DKASC dataset (specific list not in abstract)
E3.specific_model: 1D CNN, Bi-LSTM, Stacked LSTM, ANN, Linear Regression, SVR, XGBoost, and a hybrid CNN-LSTM
E3.baselines: The seven other models in the comparison
E3.metrics: MAE, explained variance, RMSE, R2, sMAPE
E3.best_reported_metric: Stacked LSTM best: MAE 1.1157, RMSE 2.3408, explained variance 0.8998, R2 0.9004, sMAPE 1.1795 (averaged across the four sequences)
E3.weather_conditions_considered: Not stated in retrieved abstract; four data sequences are used but not characterised as weather regimes
E3.external_validation: Partial - four distinct sequences act as repeated evaluation slices of one site
E3.main_contribution: Benchmarks eight models including four classical ones on four DKASC sequences and reports sMAPE alongside MAE/RMSE/R2, which is the more defensible metric choice for a zero-containing target.
E3.main_limitation: All four sequences come from one site, so between-site and between-climate generalisation is untested; no weather stratification despite using four separate sequences.
E3.research_gap: Demonstrates correct metric practice (sMAPE) and a broad model sweep, yet still analyses only one site and no weather regimes - showing that good metric hygiene has not been paired with robustness evaluation.
E3.reproducibility: Good - named public dataset (DKASC), explicit model list and full metric set

F1.input_variables: Input features compressed by an auto-encoder into a dense latent representation, concatenated back with the original features
F1.weather_variables: Meteorological features (specific list not in abstract)
F1.specific_model: AE-BiLSTM-QR: auto-encoder feature enhancement, BiLSTM temporal modelling, and quantile regression with an Incremental Monotonicity Enforcement (IME) mechanism producing non-crossing prediction intervals
F1.baselines: Several baseline models (not enumerated in abstract)
F1.metrics: Interval reliability, sharpness and mathematical coherence; probabilistic forecasting metrics (not enumerated in abstract)
F1.best_reported_metric: Intervals reported as more reliable, sharper and mathematically coherent than baselines (numbers not in abstract)
F1.uncertainty: Yes - this is the paper's central contribution; quantile regression with enforced monotonicity
F1.main_contribution: Addresses the quantile-crossing problem directly by predicting a baseline plus non-negative increments, yielding coherent prediction intervals from a hybrid deep model.
F1.main_limitation: Very recent (0 citations at time of verification) and interval calibration is reported without a named coverage metric such as PICP or PINAW in the abstract, so sharpness/reliability cannot be independently judged.
F1.research_gap: Probabilistic work exists but does not report standard calibration metrics in the abstract, and is not paired with deterministic benchmarks on a common split - limiting comparability.
F1.reproducibility: Low to moderate - architecture described; code and data not released per abstract

F2.forecast_target: PV power probability density function (full PDF)
F2.dataset: Data from a PV station in Hebei Province, China
F2.dataset_size: One PV station (record count not stated in abstract)
F2.input_variables: Meteorological, power and coefficient-vector cross-modal inputs
F2.weather_variables: Meteorological variables (specific list not in abstract)
F2.model_family: Probabilistic / distribution-free deep learning with transformer
F2.specific_model: BS-iMCFormer - B-spline approximation of a KDE-derived PDF combined with an iTransformer and multi-head cross attention; predicts B-spline control points then interpolates to a PDF
F2.metrics: KL divergence, MAE, RMSE, R2, visual PDF overlap
F2.best_reported_metric: KL divergence reduced by 54.82%; MAE and RMSE reduced by 68.93% and 69.42%; R2 improved by 6.76%
F2.uncertainty: Yes - central contribution; distribution-free PDF forecasting avoids parametric assumptions
F2.main_contribution: Removes the parametric distribution assumption common to probabilistic PV methods by representing the PDF through B-spline control points predicted by a transformer with cross-modal attention.
F2.main_limitation: Complex three-stage pipeline (KDE, spline coefficient prediction, interpolation) whose added cost is never reported; the headline MAE/RMSE reductions come with no deterministic baseline on a common split.
F2.research_gap: Uncertainty research is architecturally sophisticated but does not report computational cost or compare against simple conformal/quantile baselines, so the accuracy-cost trade-off is unknown.
F2.reproducibility: Low to moderate - method described in detail; code not released per abstract

F3.dataset: Solar power generation data (source not stated in abstract)
F3.input_variables: Meteorological and derived features; feature identities discussed via XAI
F3.weather_variables: Weather-related features (specific list not in abstract)
F3.specific_model: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, Decision Tree, each paired with three XAI methods
F3.baselines: The other tree ensembles in the comparison
F3.best_reported_metric: LightGBM best: RMSE 0.088, MSE 0.007749, MAE 0.052896, R2 0.842645
F3.explainability: Yes - this is the paper's central contribution: SHAP, LIME and Permutation Feature Importance applied across five models
F3.main_contribution: Applies three distinct XAI techniques to five tree ensembles and articulates their complementary roles: permutation importance identifies key features, SHAP reveals feature interactions, LIME provides local explanations.
F3.main_limitation: Only tree ensembles are explained, so the findings do not transfer to the recurrent or attention architectures that dominate the rest of the corpus; no explanation-faithfulness validation is reported.
F3.research_gap: Explainability is confined to interpretable model families and validated only qualitatively, so the black-box architectures that most need explanation remain unexamined.
F3.reproducibility: Moderate - models and XAI methods explicit; dataset not shared per abstract

F4.forecast_horizon: Five horizons from 4 hours to 7 days (multi-horizon)
F4.dataset: Open-source datasets from four utility-scale plants in northern China and one aggregated plant in central Australia
F4.dataset_location: Northern China (4 plants) and central Australia (1 aggregated plant)
F4.input_variables: Historical generation data fused with forward-looking inputs: numerical weather prediction, satellite-derived irradiance, and AI-based weather model forecasts
F4.weather_variables: NWP, satellite-derived irradiance, AI weather model forecasts (three distinct forecast sources)
F4.specific_model: Cross-Unet - Transformer-based architecture with multi-scale temporal encoding, correlation-aware channel attention, and hierarchical cross-attention decoding
F4.baselines: Ten deep learning baselines plus traditional operational benchmarks
F4.metrics: Forecast accuracy metrics (not enumerated in abstract); horizon-resolved comparison
F4.best_reported_metric: Outperforms ten deep learning baselines and traditional operational benchmarks across the majority of evaluated configurations spanning five plants, five horizons and three forecast sources (absolute values not in abstract)
F4.weather_conditions_considered: Not stated as named regimes; conditions varied implicitly through the three forecast sources and five horizons
F4.explainability: Partial - channel attention provides architectural interpretability, but attention weights are not validated as explanations
F4.multi_site_validation: Yes - five plants across two countries
F4.main_contribution: The most rigorous benchmark in this corpus: five horizons (4 h to 7 days) x five plants x three forecast sources, against ten deep baselines and operational benchmarks, re-evaluating architectural choices and emphasising full encoder-decoder designs and channel-dependence modelling.
F4.main_limitation: Does not report weather-regime-stratified accuracy, uncertainty quantification, or computational cost, so robustness under specific conditions and the accuracy-cost trade-off remain unquantified.
F4.research_gap: Even the most rigorous multi-horizon, multi-site benchmark in the literature omits regime-stratified evaluation, uncertainty quantification and cost reporting - showing these are systematically absent rather than merely rare.
F4.reproducibility: Good - datasets described as open-source, full experimental grid stated; code availability not stated in abstract
